common_name: Claire Grace Beebalm (Mildew-Resistant Wild Bergamot Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Claire Grace is a Mt. Cuba Center-recommended selection of native wild bergamot chosen for superior powdery mildew resistance and strong pollinator appeal compared to the straight species.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing good air circulation between plants. Claire Grace is a selection of native wild bergamot (Monarda fistulosa) chosen for improved resistance to the powdery mildew that disfigures most bee balm cultivars by midsummer in humid climates, while retaining the lavender-pink flowers and strong, sweet-mint fragrance that make wild bergamot such a magnet for bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. It tends to be more heat- and drought-tolerant than the red-flowered Monarda didyma cultivars, reflecting its origin from a species native to drier prairie and meadow habitat across much of North America. Established clumps bloom over a long season from early to midsummer and spread gradually by rhizome to form an expanding colony, so give it room or plan to divide every few years to keep it in bounds. Cut plants back by half in late spring if a more compact, later-blooming plant is desired, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor and airflow, which further reduces mildew pressure.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Monarda Trial Garden Report
North Carolina State Extension — Bee Balm Cultivar Selection
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Monarda fistulosa

common_name: Gardenview Scarlet Beebalm (Classic Tall Red Bee Balm)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Gardenview Scarlet is a classic tall red bee balm cultivar with better mildew tolerance and vigor than many older red selections, though it still benefits from good air circulation in humid Gulf South summers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Gardenview Scarlet is a long-established red bee balm cultivar valued for its large, vivid scarlet-red flower heads held on tall, sturdy stems, making it a reliable hummingbird and butterfly magnet for the summer border. It generally shows better vigor and somewhat improved mildew resistance compared to older heirloom red Monarda didyma selections, though like most red bee balms it still benefits from good air circulation, morning sun with some afternoon shade in the hottest climates, and consistent soil moisture to minimize powdery mildew in humid Gulf South summers. The aromatic, mint-scented foliage is typical of the genus, and the plant spreads by underground stolons to form an expanding colony over time. Divide every two to three years in early spring to control spread, renew vigor, and improve air circulation within the clump. Deadhead spent flower heads to tidy the planting, though the seed heads also provide some winter interest and food for finches if left standing.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Monarda didyma Cultivars
North Carolina State Extension — Bee Balm Selection for the South
American Horticultural Society — Monarda Cultivar Trials

common_name: Raspberry Wine Beebalm (Wine-Red Mildew-Resistant Bee Balm)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Raspberry Wine is a tall, vigorous bee balm cultivar with deep wine-red flowers and notably better mildew resistance than many older red and pink Monarda didyma selections.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Raspberry Wine is a vigorous bee balm cultivar bearing large, shaggy flower heads in a deep, rich wine-red color, held on tall, sturdy stems above aromatic, mint-scented foliage. It shows notably better resistance to powdery mildew than many older red and pink Monarda didyma cultivars, an important trait in the humid Gulf South where mildew commonly disfigures bee balm foliage by midsummer, though good air circulation and consistent moisture still help keep it looking its best through the season. Hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies visit the tubular flowers heavily from early to midsummer. Like other bee balms, it spreads by underground stolons to form an expanding clump; divide every two to three years in early spring to control spread, renew vigor, and reduce crowding that can encourage mildew. Deadhead spent flowers to tidy the plant, or leave some seed heads standing for winter interest and finch forage.

common_name: Cinderella Swamp Milkweed (Deep Rose-Pink Native Milkweed Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall (seeds need 30-day cold stratification) or cold-stratify indoors and start in late winter; Cinderella is a selection of native swamp milkweed chosen for larger flower clusters in a deeper rose-pink than the wild species, tolerating wet soil where many milkweeds struggle.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Cinderella is a selection of native swamp milkweed bred for larger, showier clusters of deep rose-pink flowers than the wild species, while retaining swamp milkweed's essential value as a monarch butterfly host plant and its unusual tolerance of consistently wet soil, where common milkweed and butterfly weed both struggle. Flowers bloom over a long season from early to late summer and draw monarchs, swallowtails, and bumblebees in heavy numbers. Unlike some milkweed species, it does not spread aggressively by rhizome and stays in well-behaved clumps, making it one of the easiest milkweeds to place in a mixed border, rain garden, or pond margin without it taking over. Leave seedpods standing through fall and winter for wildlife interest and natural reseeding, or deadhead spent flowers to prevent excess self-sowing. Cut back in late winter before new growth emerges.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Swamp Milkweed
Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center — Native Milkweed Selection

common_name: Ice Ballet Milkweed (White-Flowered Swamp Milkweed Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall (seeds need 30-day cold stratification) or cold-stratify indoors and start in late winter; Ice Ballet is a pure white-flowered selection of native swamp milkweed, valued equally as a monarch host plant and as a striking, non-pink alternative for white or pastel garden schemes.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Ice Ballet is a selection of native swamp milkweed bred for pure white flower clusters, a striking departure from the rose-pink of the wild species, while retaining all of swamp milkweed's value as an essential monarch butterfly host plant and its unusual tolerance of consistently wet soil, where common milkweed and butterfly weed both struggle. The clean white flowers, fragrant and produced over a long season from early to late summer, work especially well in white or pastel garden schemes and moon gardens, and they draw monarchs, swallowtails, and bumblebees just as effectively as the pink-flowered species. Like other swamp milkweed selections, it stays in well-behaved clumps rather than spreading aggressively by rhizome, making it easy to place in a mixed border, rain garden, or pond margin. Leave seedpods standing through fall and winter for wildlife interest and natural reseeding, or deadhead spent flowers to limit self-sowing. Cut back in late winter before new growth emerges.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Swamp Milkweed
Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center — Native Milkweed Selection
